text_blocks.snippet: Yes, Long COVID is still happening. While the number of new cases may have decreased since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, Long COVID remains a significant public health concern affecting millions of adults and children, according to the CDC. Anyone who gets COVID-19 can develop Long COVID, and some individuals are more susceptible than others. Symptoms can range from mild to severe and may require comprehensive care.

text_blocks.snippet: Long COVID research has progressed significantly, revealing it's not a single disease but a range of conditions with diverse underlying mechanisms. While a specific cure remains elusive, ongoing research is exploring various treatment options and strategies for managing symptoms.
Here's a more detailed look at the updates:

list.title: Multiple Endotypes:
list.snippet: Long COVID is now understood to be an umbrella term for different conditions triggered by the initial SARS-CoV-2 infection, rather than a single disease.

list.title: Diverse Mechanisms:
list.snippet: Studies have identified potential root causes, including persistent viral reservoirs, autoimmune reactions, tissue damage, and reactivation of latent viruses like Epstein-Barr.

list.title: Heterogeneity:
list.snippet: The diverse mechanisms help explain why symptoms vary widely among individuals, with some experiencing primarily neurological issues, others cardiovascular or gastrointestinal problems, and some hormonal imbalances.

list.title: Ongoing Research:
list.snippet: Scientists are actively exploring treatments targeting the various mechanisms believed to contribute to long COVID.

list.title: Symptom Management:
list.snippet: Focus remains on managing and alleviating symptoms, as specific cures are still under development.

list.title: Specific Treatments:
list.snippet: Research is exploring treatments for different endotypes, including those targeting viral persistence, autoimmune responses, and tissue repair.

list.title: Hormonal Changes:
list.snippet: Research has identified hormonal changes associated with long COVID, including lower cortisol levels and, in females, lower testosterone levels, according to the American Medical Association.

list.title: Continued Monitoring:
list.snippet: Long COVID research is ongoing, and continued monitoring and updates are expected as scientists learn more about this complex condition, according to the IDSA.
